entries.title: What to know about diarrhea-causing cyclosporiasis in Illinois
entries.summary: <p>Illinois has confirmed 995 confirmed and probable cases of the diarrhea-causing illness cyclosporiasis, the state’s public health department confirmed Tuesday.</p><p>Cyclosporiasis is not considered deadly and is more of an inconvenience that in rare cases could have complications, said Dr. Emily Landon, an infectious diseases specialist at University of Chicago Medicine. In Illinois, 58 people have been hospitalized, according to the Illinois Department of Public Health. Most of the people in Illinois who have contracted the illness had traveled recently — 193 people internationally and 631<b> </b>domestically. It’s unclear if the other 171 traveled.</p><p>Higher numbers of cyclosporiasis are typically reported in the summer, but this year has seen an especially high number, health officials said.</p><p>The increase in Illinois is part of a larger number of cases in several states. In Michigan, which has been at the center of an outbreak nationally, two people with significant health conditions died, health officials announced on Aug. 3, saying that cyclosporiasis and dehydration contributed to the deaths. The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services is reporting <a class="Link" href="https://www.michigan.gov/mdhhs/keep-mi-healthy/infectious-diseases/infectious-disease-outbreaks" target="_blank" >12,218 cases</a> as of Wednesday. Across the country, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reports just 1,947 cases in nine states, which is far less than Michigan alone. Those cases were linked to eating at Taco Bell, according to the CDC and the FDA. <b></b></p><p>Here's what you need to know about cyclosporiasis in Illinois.</p><h3><b>What is cyclosporiasis?</b></h3><p>Pronounced sigh-klo-spore-EYE-uh-sis, cyclosporiasis is an intestinal illness caused by the microscopic parasite cyclospora. Infection often comes after eating fresh fruits and vegetables and can lead to watery diarrhea, stomach cramps, gas and nausea.</p><p>The heat-loving parasite infects the bowels and spreads through feces. In the past, people have been infected by consuming fruits or vegetables that were exposed to feces-contaminated irrigation water. </p><h3><b>What is causing cyclosporiasis in Illinois?</b></h3><p>No definitive source has been identified for the Illinois cases, but public health officials have been investigating a link to iceberg lettuce. Taylor Fresh Foods, a California-based farm and food company, on July 17 voluntarily recalled iceberg salad and shredded lettuce products distributed in 27 states, including Illinois. In other states, Marketside-brand iceberg products sold at select Walmart stores were also recalled. </p><p>The FDA on July 19 said that initial testing for cyclospora in a sample of lettuce from Taylor Farms was a false positive. The products in question from Taylor Farms were grown in the Mexican state of Guanajuato. The FDA encourages the public to avoid eating any products recalled by Taylor Farms, and the CDC recommends that anyone who purchased the recalled lettuce should throw it out.</p><p>The voluntary recall came after the <a class="Link" href="https://www.cdc.gov/cyclosporiasis/outbreaks/07-26/index.html" target="_blank" >CDC</a> identified shredded lettuce served at Taco Bell locations in Indiana, Michigan, Kentucky, Ohio and West Virginia as a source of widespread outbreaks in those states. Taco Bell removed the affected lettuce from its supply chain across the country and planned to replace it in select states, the company previously said. Taylor Farms supplied lettuce to Taco Bell, The New York Times reported.</p><p>The CDC is also investigating other cases of cyclosporiasis that are not connected to the national outbreak.</p><p>Past outbreaks have been linked to imported fresh produce, like bagged salad kits and berries, according to IDPH. Cyclosporiasis is not transmitted from person to person, Landon said. Even if a person becomes sick, people don’t usually contaminate objects in their house enough to spread it to someone else.</p><h3><b>How long does it take to recover?</b></h3><p>People should talk to their doctor about getting tested if they have symptoms, so health officials can continue to track the outbreak, said Gwen Biggerstaff, the CDC’s deputy director of foodborne, waterborne and environmental diseases.</p><p>Most people who contract the illness recover in one to two weeks, according to the CDC. Many can recover with rest and plenty of fluids, but some may need antibiotics.</p><p>People can experience bloating, gas and dehydration but rarely have more complications.</p><p>“The problem with this disease is it can be kind of persistent,” Landon said. “And you can feel pretty sick, and then you can be starting to get better, and then the diarrhea can come back again.” </p><h3><b>Should I stop eating fresh fruits and vegetables? </b></h3><p>If a person is immunocompromised or has an underlying medical condition, they should take more precautions, Landon said. That’s especially true, for example, for those undergoing surgery soon or cancer treatments.</p><p>Everyone can follow typical food safety guidelines like washing hands and thoroughly washing and scrubbing fresh produce. Illinois health officials also suggest:</p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-b5494250-808c-11f1-a776-3b92d1e3bbf6"><li>Incorporating more fruits and vegetables with peels or outer layers</li><li>Eating canned fruits and vegetables</li><li>Keeping produce separate from raw meat and seafood</li><li>Refrigerating cut, peeled, or cooked fruits and vegetables within two hours</li><li>Refrigerating perishable produce.</li><li>Cooking vegetables to at least 158 degrees Fahrenheit </li></ul><h3><b>Is it safer to buy produce from my local Illinois farmers market? </b></h3><p>Fruits and vegetables coming from a smaller, local producer are likely to have less of a risk for contamination than food from massive manufacturers, Landon said. That’s especially true if an outbreak is centered on a certain product, but officials this time around don’t know if that’s the case.</p><p>So you shouldn’t assume there’s zero risk in buying from a local vendor because any farm can become contaminated, especially because of the current weather, Landon said.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><h3><b>How is Illinois tracking the cases?</b></h3><p>The Illinois Department of Public Health is working with local health officials to collect data on the cases. They are also working with the CDC to investigate a potential source of the illness.</p><p>The Chicago Department of Public Health has not identified the source of local cases. One individual had eaten at Taco Bell but had also traveled to one of the states that is part of the larger outbreak. The department is seeing an increase in cases among Latinos who had not recently traveled internationally.</p><p>The number of cases locally and across the country could be higher, Landon said. That’s because testing for cyclosporiasis is expensive, and some insurance may not cover it. But as cases of cyclosporiasis are more in the news, doctors will likely start testing more patients or prescribe antibiotics to treat it if someone has symptoms.</p><p>If a person is confirmed to have cyclosporiasis, Landon said it’s important to cooperate with the local health department to detail everything they ate so officials can pinpoint the outbreak source.</p><h3><b>Are federal cuts affecting the outbreak? </b></h3><p>Last summer, the federal government scaled back a program known as the Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network that monitored foodborne illnesses, <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-news/cdc-quietly-scaled-back-surveillance-program-foodborne-illnesses-rcna227089?link_source=ta_bluesky_link&taid=68add0b9b2316600014ce6de&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_medium=social&utm_source=bluesky" target="_blank" ><u>NBC News previously reported</u></a>. As part of the changes, reporting for cyclospora parasites became optional in 2025, according to the program’s website. The government had previously collected that data since 1997.</p><p>The scaled-back federal program worked with the FDA to proactively test certain foods to check if recalls were necessary, Landon said.</p><p>It’s hard to assess how much changes on the federal level are playing a role in the current outbreaks, Landon said. But it’s something health officials across the country should consider.</p><p>“It’s a combination of the nature of the illness, the fact that it’s happening at a time when there’s other sporadic cases, and then the lack of infrastructure and resources available for testing does matter,” Landon said, summing up the factors driving the outbreak. <br></p>

entries.title: 'Stone-cold killer' linked to slayings of 2 teen girlfriends was caught on jailhouse wire: prosecutors
entries.summary: <p>Paranoid his girlfriend was betraying him to a rival gang, Anthony Nunnally allegedly shot and killed her in an East Side alley last October, prosecutors said in court Wednesday.</p><p>Just over a year before that, he allegedly killed another girlfriend in a different East Side alley in September 2024, shooting her several times. </p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/04/anthony-nunnally-gabriella-arellano-sierra-evans" target="_blank" >21-year-old was charged this week </a>with two counts of first-degree murder for their deaths. On Wednesday afternoon, Cook County Circuit Court Judge Deidre Dyer ordered him detained until trial.</p><p>Nunnally was already in Cook County jail for an unrelated carjacking charge. He allegedly tried to steal the car of a friend from grade school last October, around the time of the second killing, Cook County prosecutors said in court Wednesday. </p><p>At one point during his incarceration, his cellmate was a former member of the Latin Kings, the Chicago street gang to which Nunnally also allegedly belongs. The cellmate, wearing a wire, got Nunnally talking about the October 2025 murder, Cook County Assistant State's Attorney Mike Pekara said in court. </p><p>Unaware he was being recorded, Nunnally told his cellmate that he was paranoid his 17-year-old girlfriend, Gabriella Arellano, was going to "backdoor him," slang for betraying him to a rival gang. </p><p>When the cellmate asked if he felt any remorse for killing her, Nunnally allegedly said: "When some b - - - - backdoor you, you gotta do what you gotta do," according to Pekara. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/10/26/woman-shot-east-side" target="_blank" >Arellano was found shot once in the head</a> in an alley in the 11000 block of South Mackinaw Avenue on Oct. 26, 2025. Prosecutors said Wednesday that a nearby Ring camera captured the sound of the gunshot and then Nunnally and an unknown person running from the area. Another surveillance camera showed Nunnally, Arellano and the unknown person in the area before the girl was killed. </p><h3>2024 murder</h3><p>About a year earlier, on Sept. 28, 2024, 19-year-old <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2024/09/28/woman-found-shot-to-death-on-far-south-side" target="_blank" >Sierra Evans was found shot</a> several times in the 9500 block of South Avenue N. Evans and Nunnally had been dating for about a month at the time she was killed, Pekara said. </p><p>The night she died, Evans, Nunnally and two other people were drinking and hanging out in a basement, Pekara said. At one point in the night, Nunnally allegedly got angry with Evans and choked and pinned her against a wall. He also punched a hole in the wall of the basement, at which point he was kicked out of the house, Pekara said. </p><p>Later, he called the two people and said he was in an Uber on his way back to the house, Pekara said. Minutes later, they heard several gunshots. Nunnally came running into the basement, holding a gun. He said he just killed someone and then flashed a gang sign. He did not say he killed Evans, Pekara said. </p><p>Evans was found the next day in a nearby alley with 18 shell casings next to her body. </p><p>About seven months later, Nunnally was allegedly threatening to hurt a new girlfriend. He pulled up a TV news clip of a memorial service for a Evans and told the new girlfriend he was going to do the same thing to her that he did to Evans, according to Pekara. </p><p>Scott Kozicki, the Cook County public defender representing Nunnally, said in court that prosecutors didn't have enough evidence proving Nunnally shot both girls. </p><p>In the 2024 slaying, Kozicki said there was no evidence that the gun Nunnally came into the basement with matched the shell casings found at the crime scene. He also questioned the ability of the Ring camera to pick up the sound of a gunshot from the 2025 murder. </p><p>As for the confession to the Chicago street gang member, Kozicki said it was "really shaky, problematic entrapment." He added that Nunnally's cellmate had a great motive to sell him out. </p><p>"These are a lot of scary stories, but being near gunshots does not mean you participated in a shooting," Kozicki said. </p><p>Pekara pushed back against that claim. </p><p>Nunnally "was the person last seen with each of these young women before they died. He was seen with a gun seconds after the first murder. In the second murder, the Ring camera got the sound of a gunshot and saw [Nunnally] running away," Pekara said. </p><p>"He is a stone-cold killer," Pekara added. "This is not a scary story, it’s a fact."</p>

entries.title: Pritzker asks oil CEOs to return Iran war windfall profits to Illinois consumers: 'You owe it to the people'
entries.summary: <p>Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker on Wednesday penned letters to the U.S. CEOs of seven major oil companies, accusing them of "profiteering" from the war in Iran and imploring them to return windfall profits to Illinois consumers, among other demands.</p><p>It's a rare agreement between the Democratic governor and President Donald Trump, who on Monday railed against Chevron and Exxon Mobil for high profits amid the Iran war and said they should "give some of that back to the public."</p><p>"Under the guise of supply disruptions from war in the Middle East, your companies are collecting windfall profits from the hardworking families and businesses in Illinois," <a class="Link" href="https://cms.chicago.suntimes.com/cms/content/edit.jsp?id=0000019f-d309-dc99-abff-df9b8d6f0000&typeId=8195a523-335e-3fbb-a4c1-12dbad30b87e" target="_blank" >Pritzker writes in the letter</a> to the CEOs of Shell, Exxon Mobil Corp., Chevron Corp., Continental Resources Inc., bp America, ConocoPhillips and Occidental Petroleum Corp. "That’s the very definition of profiteering, and you owe it to the people of my state and the nation to disgorge those excess profits and provide meaningful price relief to consumers."</p><p>American oil and gas companies are making massive profits while fighting between the U.S. and Iran hinders petroleum shipments. That has led to consumers worldwide paying more for fuel. The conflict has halted most shipping through of Strait of Hormuz, which serves as a delivery route for a large portion of the world's oil and natural gas supply. </p><p>Trump has criticized oil companies' stark profits, writing in June on social media that he wanted the Justice Department to investigate whether "customers are being 'gouged.'" Trump reiterated that claim in the Oval Office Monday, saying he's not happy with the profits reported by Chevron and Exxon Mobil, even though the higher margins reflected energy prices that increased after Trump launched the war, the Associated Press reported. </p><p>“They made too much money, too much money, “ Trump said. “They ought to give some of that back to the public, and they better cut the retail price.”</p><p>Oil companies don't set the price at the pump, but gas station operators have to raise prices when the cost of oil surges, as it has during the Iran war. </p><p>Pritzker's letter to the CEOs says their businesses are profiting "while families across my state and the nation face sharply higher prices at the pump." Since the war began, the price of regular gasoline in Illinois has risen by more than $1.30 per gallon, averaging $4.34 per gallon statewide and costing residents an additional $2 billion so far, the governor wrote. </p><p>The governor wants CEOs to state whether their company is preparing to return any portion of profits to Illinois consumers via price reductions, direct refunds or other means. He also asks them to provide refining margins and wholesale pricing decisions, as well as detailed information about their refinery and operational decisions that affected the volume of gasoline and diesel fuel available to consumers. Pritzker also is seeking information about executive compensation.</p><p>"Illinoisans have a right to know how your companies are profiting from this conflict, how much of those outsized profits Illinois families are being made to pay, and what steps you will now take to provide them with relief at the pump," Pritzker writes.</p><p>The governor is asking for a response from the CEOs by Aug. 21. <br></p>

entries.title: 'Not OK for us': Bears' offense urgently needs to get back on track as sloppy mistakes resurface
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> have seen worse — way worse — from their offense than this, so it’s not cause for alarm. But it is mildly concerning that quarterback Caleb Williams and his group backslid after a strong start to training camp.</p><p>Ever since they started practicing in pads Monday, the offense hasn’t quite looked right, and while some of that is bound to happen throughout the marathon of camp, the pre-snap hiccups are something the Bears thought they’d buried last season.</p><p>The upside is that, as usual, coach Ben Johnson’s staff isn’t sugarcoating or spinning it. The first step toward fixing a problem is being honest about where it stands, and these coaches don’t have any hesitation to call it out.</p><p>“We've taken a step back, honestly, in our pre-snap communication,” offensive coordinator Press Taylor said before practice Wednesday morning. “A lot of times just not being on the same page, not seeing something the same way, not communicating... It can expose you if you're not ready.”</p><p>Taylor mentioned snags in calling the play in the huddle, breaking the huddle and being disciplined at the line of scrimmage, where Johnson uses many shifts and motions that can lead to false starts or delay-of-game penalties if the offense isn’t sharp.</p><p>All of that was hammered to offensive players in a meeting Tuesday and the evening walk-through. Wednesday wasn’t really the day to show they’d fixed those issues since the team held a very short and light practice without pads, but the Bears will be full-go Thursday morning, and that will reveal a lot about the offense’s ability to regroup.</p><p>None of it has been as bad as it was last August, when the Bears embarrassed themselves at the Family Fest practice at Soldier Field. That was their 10th practice of camp, and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/03/bears-coach-ben-johnson-sends-qb-caleb-williams-offense-stern-message-about-sloppy-mistakes" >it was such a disaster offensively that Johnson fired a warning shot</a> to the team: “If it continues like that, we’re not going to win many games.”</p><p>It did, in fact, continue like that for quite a while. The Bears closed the preseason with an equally discouraging performance against the Chiefs, rife with errors and sloppiness, then sputtered to an 0-2 start in the regular season.</p><p>The Bears committed the fourth-most false starts (33) and illegal-formation penalties (five) last season, plus five delay-of-game penalties, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.nflpenalties.com/" target="_blank" >NFLPenalties.com</a>. Those do more damage than just a handful of yards. They can be drive wreckers by putting the team in second- or third-and-long.</p><p>Throughout training camp last year, Johnson was constantly on Williams about being too slow to get out of the huddle and not keeping the group in sync at the line of scrimmage. They’re much more on the same page now, but there have still been some slipups this week. And this was one element that should’ve looked good from the jump.</p><p>“He has the ability to elevate his play,” Taylor said of Williams. “We need just the consistency down in, down out, the communication in the huddle, out of the huddle, at the line. That’s something that will always be a continued process for Caleb.”</p><p>Johnson said this week there have been “way too many mistakes” and “little things like that start to accumulate,” but was evenhanded in his overall assessment that an increase in missteps was “probably normal with the volume [of plays] continuing to increase, yet it's not OK for us and we're going to nip that in the bud.”</p><p>The Bears still have more than a month to work out these glitches before their season opener at the Panthers, but they aren’t going to get to the more advanced concepts of Johnson’s offense if they’re still stumbling. And while he’s been measured and patience in his reactions so far, he’ll have no reservations about getting a lot louder if necessary.</p>

entries.title: Conductor que iba en sentido contrario en expressway intentaba 'asustar' a mujer que suplicaba por su vida
entries.summary: <p>Un hombre de Aurora permanecía el martes bajo custodia, un día después de que los fiscales afirmaran que manejó en sentido contrario por la autopista Dan Ryan para "asustar" a una mujer que suplicaba por su vida momentos antes de morir a causa de un choque en el que estuvieron involucrados cinco vehículos.</p><p>Juan Ruiz Huerta, de 29 años de edad, fue acusado de asesinato en primer grado, secuestro, privación ilegal de la libertad y agresión agravada <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/31/dan-ryan-crash" target="_blank" >relacionada con el choque del viernes por la noche</a> que mató a la residente de Chicago, Victory A. Swanigan, de 28 años, y dejó a otro conductor gravemente herido.</p><p>Un juez del Condado de Cook ordenó que Ruiz Huerta permaneciera bajo custodia durante una audiencia el lunes en la Corte Penal Leighton. Debe regresar a la corte el 19 de agosto.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-1e0000" name="module-1e0000"></a> <div pretendiendo románticamente durante meses y que la recogió después de una cita en el salón de belleza que él pagó, cuando se enojó con ella por el "estado de su relación".</p><p>Poco después de las 5:30 p.m. del viernes, Ruiz Huerta ingresó a la Interestatal 94 y arrebasó a vehículos que se desplazaban lentamente y a luces policiales al norte de 31st Street, donde Swanigan gritó pidiendo ayuda, dijeron los fiscales.</p><p>Luego Ruiz Huerta dio una vuelta en U y empezó a conducir a alta velocidad hacia el sur por los carriles de sentido norte de la I-94, mientras la amiga de Swanigan pudo escucharse a sí misma suplicándole que redujera la velocidad, según los fiscales.</p><p>Swanigan le dijo a Ruiz Huerta que tenía "tres hijos a los que quería volver a ver" mientras él seguía acelerando, según dijeron los fiscales.</p><p>Un video de vigilancia de la Autoridad de Tránsito de Chicago (CTA) en 47th Street captó a Ruiz Huerta moviéndose a través de varios carriles a alta velocidad y zigzagueando entre numerosos autos y camiones que circulaban en la dirección correcta, antes de chocar frontalmente con otro automóvil que iba hacia el norte por los carriles exprés y provocar que el vehículo de Ruiz Huerta volcara sobre el separador de concreto y cayera a los carriles locales, según documentos de la corte.</p><p>Los fiscales señalaron que el otro conductor en el choque —que sufrió múltiples fracturas de costillas, una laceración en el hígado y otras lesiones— dijo a los investigadores que intentó cambiar de carril para evitar el choque cuando Ruiz Huerta también cambió de carril.</p><p>El informe de una orden de registro ejecutada en la caja negra del Mazda CX-5 2013 de Ruiz-Huerta mostró que viajaba a 86 millas por hora cinco segundos antes del choque y que al momento del impacto, iba a 78 millas por hora sin que hubiera presión en el freno y con el acelerador presionado al 25%, dijeron las autoridades.</p><p>Swanigan, quien residía en la cuadra 8800 al sur de Normal Avenue en el vecindario de Auburn Gresham, fue declarada muerta en la escena, según la Policía Estatal de Illinois y la Oficina del Médico Forense del Condado de Cook.</p><p>Ruiz Huerta supuestamente les dijo a los agentes que, una vez que supo que Swanigan estaba aterrorizada, él la "puso en peligro para obtener una respuesta de ella" sobre el estado de su relación.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" entries.title: 'Fail Mary' in mind, Bears CB Tyrique Stevenson still seeking consistency
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> cornerback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/05/bears-lb-t-j-edwards-returns-to-practice-after-missing-first-week-with-calf-injury" target="_blank" >Tyrique Stevenson</a> mentions the “Fail Mary” before you have a chance to.</p><p>One mistake, he said, can get you cast aside by the rest of the NFL. He’s lived it.</p><p>“One play could just … As far as injury, as far as mistakes, as far as anything, this league will forget about you in a heartbeat,” he told the Sun-Times earlier this week. “For me, it’s just constantly sitting on my brain every time I touch the field — ‘Just go out there and lay it on the line and stay focused.’</p><p>“I think for that, that’s how I look at it, just an internal motivation. Every play matters. <i>Every play matters</i>.”</p><p>That’s especially true for Stevenson, whether it’s a training camp snap or the last throw of a 2024 loss against the Commanders. That misplay — Stevenson had his back to the ball, jawing at fans, before misplaying Jayden Daniels’ 52-yard game-winning heave — will follow Stevenson for the rest of his career. His goal is to make it feel, eventually, like more of a footnote.</p><p>“From the Hail Mary, my mindset is, go out here every play and show who you can be, and dominate,” he said, “and everything will fall in line.”</p><p>He knows the stakes in Year 4. So do the Bears.</p><p>Defensive coordinator Dennis Allen can put on tape from Stevenson last year that was astoundingly good — and then watch lapses that were maddening. Coaches spent the offseason urging Stevenson to become the steady presence the defense sorely needs.</p><p>“Tyrique needs to be more consistent,” Allen said.</p><p>That goes beyond the practice field, coach Ben Johnson said. He’s seen growth in Stevenson since the end of last season, when he took a backseat to the team’s two starting outside cornerbacks.</p><p>“It’s really the focus level from being in the building, paying attention in meetings and continuing to apply that on the field throughout a two-plus hour practice,” Johnson said. “So I think we’ve seen strides there. It’s certainly improving … He knows it. So we’re pretty happy with where he’s at.”</p><p>Stevenson has been working at it. Stability in his personal life — he got engaged July 4 — has allowed him to focus his attention on his tasks inside Halas Hall.</p><p>“You have everything on the outside complete,” he said, “so let’s turn around and go be an all-pro.”</p><p>Despite posting the best Pro Football Focus grades of any of his three seasons, Stevenson’s playing time dwindled last season. Counting the playoffs, Stevenson didn’t start five out of the 15 games in which he was healthy. In his first two seasons, he started all but two of 32 — and one was the oh-so-brief benching after the “Fail Mary.” Stevenson played just 18 defensive snaps in Week 17 and none in Week 18. He appeared in 14 snaps in the Bears’ playoff win against the Packers and 18 in their loss to the Rams.</p><p>For Stevenson, this season is the last chance for him to prove that he’s a reliable starter before he becomes a free agent in March. He’s run with the starters every day during training camp, with a banged-up Terell Smith and fourth-round rookie Malik Muhammad II playing behind him.</p><p>During camp practices, Stevenson is being tested by receiver Luther Burden, who’s earned praise from almost everyone inside Halas Hall this offseason, and held his own. Tuesday, he intercepted Caleb Williams after a miscommunication between the quarterback and tight end Colston Loveland.</p><p>“He's been challenging us,” Burden said. “Making plays out there.”</p><p>He’ll be targeted when games begin, too — teams will avoid throwing toward two-time Pro Bowl cornerback Jaylon Johnson, who’s recovered from last year’s groin surgery.</p><p>Stevenson has the physical skills to be dominant — that’s been apparent since the team made him the 56<sup>th</sup> pick in 2023. When he makes mistakes, he said, they’re rooted in subtleties of his technique. That comes down to focus.</p><p>“It’s one of the things I do daily to keep my mind coming back to the main point — focus and lock in and make the play you know you can make,” he said. “The frustrating part is, ‘We’ve seen you make the plays and we’ve seen you make them multiple times. So why not this time?’”</p><p>What the future holds, he’s not sure. Stevenson tries not to think about free agency. He knows it won’t help his mindset.</p><p>“I don’t want to create an extra block of worry or anxiety that’s not needed,” he said.</p><p>The Bears need him more than ever. They let cornerback Nahshon Wright, the NFL’s takeaways leader last season, leave via free agency because they believed Stevenson was ready to retake his starting role. The pressure on the position has only ratcheted up during training camp because of the injuries to slot cornerback Kyler Gordon and safety Coby Bryant. Gordon, who hurt his calf, has no timeline to return. Bryant, who hurt his knee earlier this week, will miss at least two months. Were the season to start today, Jaylon Jones, the Bears’ third-string slot cornerback, would be the starter.</p><p>Stevenson, then, needs to become the least of the Bears’ concerns.</p><p>“Tyrique is on a contract year,” Jaylon Johnson said. “He’s got to prove himself.”</p>
